newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Change rolls on 10 years after London "Big Bang".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Change rolls on 10 years after London "Big Bang".

text.p: It has been 10 years since "Big Bang" reforms jarred London financial markets and transformed its arcane, outmoded stock market into a global powerhouse.
As the "City" celebrates London's success under deregulation, it is also preparing for the next decade of change that promises to be no less dramatic than the last.

For centuries, London's financial hub was contained in one square mile where an exclusive group of men gathered to trade securities. It was a world of paper, pencils, stiff collars, and silk hats, and a place where one's word was one's bond.

Under the deregulating Conservative government of Margaret Thatcher, a series of radical reforms, known as Big Bang, spawned, among other things, the London Stock Exchange's (LSE) Seaq electronic share trading system.
In one day, Seaq swept away years of traditional dealmaking on the trading floor of Europe's busiest stock exchange and replaced it with electronic dealing rooms.

Yet just as the trading floor was abandoned 10 years ago, the next decade will see the demise of screen-based trading rooms, said Peter Cochrane, head of research at British Telecommunications (BT) Labs, which supplies much of London's financial community with computer systems.
"It's an inevitability," said Cochrane, who predicts that in as few as five years, the trading ability of computers will surpass that of humans.

BT and others are developing trading systems that add artificial intelligence, using a series of algorithms embedded in a computer that can learn from experience by constructing models of the future and making retrospective comparisons.
An algorithm is a complex mathematical formula that essentially gives directions to a computer.
These trading systems can recognise chaotic patterns and predict the next move in the market using logic, rather than emotion.
The new barons in this environment will be those who are adept in information technology, banking, marketing and in analysing trading data.

"Even today, the most successful trading firms are those that use machines with humans," said Cochrane. "Stock markets were set up about 300 years ago when societies moved very slowly. Today's markets are infinite and move very quickly."
Indeed, in increasingly competitive and complex global financial markets, trading firms with the fastest, most reliable and the best decision algorithms have the competitive advantage.

Stock exchanges will have to compete on similar terms. While the regulatory environment and the quality of an exchange's listings will continue to play a major role in attracting liquidity, "the one with the best algorithms will be the one that wins," Cochrane said.

Maintaining the status of a world financial centre, "certainly doesn't depend on geography anymore. It's regulation, of course, but also the quality of the technology, the ability to access that technology and the cost of doing business," said Michael Waller-Bridge, chief executive of Tradepoint, the upstart London-based rival to the London Stock Exchange.

Tradepoint has been fully automated since its debut a year ago. Its order-driven approach, which involves buy and sell orders being matched by computer without the need for a middle man or market-maker, sharply reduces the cost of transactions, Waller-Bridge said.

Meanwhile, the LSE, still locked in debate about detailed aspects of its reform, does not expect to replace its Seaq system and reliance on telephones and market-makers with a fully-automated quote-driven system until the fourth quarter of 1997.

Already behind in technology, some say London's status as a financial centre depends upon how quickly and far the LSE goes in automating the trading process. The LSE has said "Big Bang II" will be powered by technology.
But Martin Wheatley, head of LSE market development, said he believes the exchange's future is secure because it has critical mass, something that isn't going to disappear overnight.

"Technology is an equalising influence and it probably will lead to to a reduction in the number of exchanges in the world," said Wheatley. "But it's not the best technology or the cheapest prices, it's having critical mass."
Wheatley said the LSE's biggest and most immediate threat comes from New York, not Tradepoint or European stock exchanges.
Many believe that vast improvements in technology make the concept of a financial centre obsolete.
"A financial centre is what works where it works," said Sir David Scholey, chairman of the council of international advisory at SBC Warburg.

"What exists today is effective and sophisticated, but it's not London, or New York or Tokyo. The financial centre that exists today is a (computer) network and those cities are just components of that network," Scholey added.
